title: What is type erasure in generics, and what does it make impossible (`new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, generic arrays, overload by generic type), plus the PECS rule (`? extends` producer, `? super` consumer)?
shortTitle: What is type erasure in generics, what does it make impossible, and what is the PECS rule?

s1_definition.profdef: Type erasure is the Java compiler's process of removing generic type information after it has used it for compile-time type checking, replacing type parameters with their bounds, or with `Object` when unbounded, and inserting casts as needed. As a result the runtime sees raw types, so generics give compile-time safety with no runtime type tokens. This makes several things impossible: `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, creating generic arrays like `new T[]`, and overloading two methods that differ only by generic type argument, because after erasure their signatures collide. PECS, meaning "Producer Extends, Consumer Super," is the rule for wildcard bounds: use `? extends T` when a structure produces T values for you to read, and `? super T` when it consumes T values you write into it.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India stamps every form with a label like "this box only accepts savings-account records" while the clerk checks the forms (compile time). But once the forms are filed, the label is peeled off and every box just says "records" (runtime erasure). So later you cannot ask a filed box "were you originally the savings-only box?" because the label is gone. PECS is the handling rule: if you are reading records out of a box that might hold savings or any subtype, you label it "produces account records" so you can safely read them as accounts; if you are putting account records into a box, you label it "accepts accounts or any parent type" so your writes are always valid.
s1_definition.oneliner: Type erasure deletes generic types at runtime so new T, instanceof on a parameterized type, generic arrays, and generic-only overloads are impossible, and PECS says read with extends and write with super.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Type erasure is the Java compiler's process of removing generic type information after it has used it for compile-time type checking, replacing type parameters with their bounds, or with `Object` when unbounded, and inserting casts as needed. As a result the runtime sees raw types, so generics give compile-time safety with no runtime type tokens. This makes several things impossible: `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, creating generic arrays like `new T[]`, and overloading two methods that differ only by generic type argument, because after erasure their signatures collide. PECS, meaning "Producer Extends, Consumer Super," is the rule for wildcard bounds: use `? extends T` when a structure produces T values for you to read, and `? super T` when it consumes T values you write into it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India stamps every form with a label like "this box only accepts savings-account records" while the clerk checks the forms (compile time). But once the forms are filed, the label is peeled off and every box just says "records" (runtime erasure). So later you cannot ask a filed box "were you originally the savings-only box?" because the label is gone. PECS is the handling rule: if you are reading records out of a box that might hold savings or any subtype, you label it "produces account records" so you can safely read them as accounts; if you are putting account records into a box, you label it "accepts accounts or any parent type" so your writes are always valid.

**One line to remember:** Type erasure deletes generic types at runtime so new T, instanceof on a parameterized type, generic arrays, and generic-only overloads are impossible, and PECS says read with extends and write with super.

sections.s2_technical:
At compile time the compiler fully checks generics, so if you declare a `List<String>` it will stop you from adding an Integer. But after checking, it erases the type parameter: an unbounded `T` becomes `Object`, a bounded `T extends Number` becomes `Number`, and it inserts casts at call sites so your code still returns the right type. The consequence is that `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class, `List`, at runtime, and this single fact explains every restriction.

You cannot write `new T()` because at runtime `T` is erased to its bound, so the JVM does not know which constructor to call; the standard workaround is to pass a `Class<T>` token and use reflection, for example `clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()`. You cannot write `instanceof List<String>` because the runtime only has `List`, with no memory of the element type, so the check is meaningless; you can only test `instanceof List<?>`. You cannot create a generic array like `new T[10]` because arrays are reified, meaning they carry their component type and check it at runtime with store checks, which directly conflicts with erased generics, so the compiler forbids it and you use a `List<T>` or an `Object[]` with an unchecked cast instead. You cannot overload two methods that differ only by their generic type argument, such as one taking `List<String>` and one taking `List<Integer>`, because after erasure both become `List`, giving the same signature and a name clash.

PECS governs wildcard bounds and comes straight from how variance interacts with reading and writing. A `List<? extends Number>` is a producer: you can safely read elements as Number because whatever the exact subtype is, every element is at least a Number, but you cannot add anything except null, because the compiler does not know the exact subtype. A `List<? super Integer>` is a consumer: you can safely add Integers because whatever the exact supertype is, an Integer fits, but when you read you only get Object back, because you do not know how far up the hierarchy the list is typed. So the rule is: if a parameter is a source you take values from, use `? extends T`; if it is a sink you put values into, use `? super T`; and if you both read and write, use an exact `T` with no wildcard. The canonical example is `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`, which reads from the extends source and writes to the super destination. A senior nuance: erasure is why generics are a compile-time feature with zero runtime cost and why you get unchecked-cast warnings; it is also why you sometimes pass a Class token or a TypeReference to recover type information at runtime, and PECS is not academic, because getting the wildcard wrong is a very common cause of "cannot be applied" compile errors in real APIs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a generic repository and a method that wants to create a fresh entity instance, but `new T()` does not compile because the type is erased at runtime. This is exactly the erasure restriction — the workaround is to pass a Class token and construct reflectively.

Problem 2 — A reporting utility must sum the balances of a list that may hold Account or any subtype like SavingsAccount, and separately must deposit interest records into a list typed to Account or any supertype. This is exactly the PECS rule — read with `? extends` and write with `? super`.

The demo shows a generic repository using a Class token to instantiate, a sum method using `? extends`, a fill method using `? super`, and comments demonstrating why instanceof on a parameterized type, generic arrays, and generic-only overloads do not compile. Classes and steps: `Account` and `SavingsAccount`, `GenericRepository` (Class token), `BalanceUtil` (PECS methods), and `ErasureDemo`.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the erasure + PECS demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.generics.ErasureDemo

# See erasure for yourself: the bytecode shows raw List, no element type.
javap -c -p com.bank.generics.BalanceUtil

# Uncommenting new T(), the two process() overloads, or instanceof List<String>
# makes the module FAIL TO COMPILE — proving the erasure restrictions.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a fresh Account, a list of SavingsAccount for Rajesh and Priya, and an Account list to receive a new savings record.

Step 1 — The GenericRepository is built with the Account.class token. Because T is erased, it cannot call new T, so newEntity uses the token with reflection to construct a real Account, which the demo then stamps with SAV2001.

Step 2 — totalBalance is called with a List of SavingsAccount, which is accepted because the parameter is List of ? extends Account, a producer. The method reads each element as an Account and sums Rajesh's and Priya's balances to Rs.1,250,000, but it cannot add to the list because the exact subtype is unknown.

Step 3 — addSavings is called with a List of Account, accepted because the parameter is List of ? super SavingsAccount, a consumer. It writes a new SavingsAccount SAV9999 of Rs.500,000 into the list safely, because a SavingsAccount fits any supertype list.

Step 4 — The demo prints the erasure facts: List of String and List of Integer report the same runtime class because both erased to List, instanceof only works against List of ?, and the comments show that new T, generic arrays, and generic-only overloads would not compile, all consequences of the single erasure fact.

```
2026-10-26 16:00:01 [INFO] Created new Account via Class token
2026-10-26 16:00:01 [INFO] Total balance of 2 accounts = Rs.1250000
2026-10-26 16:00:01 [INFO] Added SavingsAccount SAV9999 into a ? super sink
2026-10-26 16:00:01 [INFO] List<String> and List<Integer> are the same runtime class: true
2026-10-26 16:00:01 [INFO] instanceof List<String> is illegal; only (strings instanceof List<?>) = true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  COMPILE TIME (types checked)              RUNTIME (types erased)
  ────────────────────────────            ───────────────────────────
  GenericRepository<Account>              GenericRepository (T → Object)
     new T() not allowed       ──►     use Class<T> token + reflection → new Account()

  List<? extends Account> (PRODUCER)      List (element type gone)
     read as Account                   for (Account a : list) sum += a.getBalance()
     add(...)                    Rajesh 1,000,000 + Priya 250,000 = 1,250,000

  List<? super SavingsAccount> (CONSUMER) List
     add(SavingsAccount)                sink.add(new SavingsAccount("SAV9999",500,000))
     read gives Object only

  List<String> vs List<Integer>  ──►  both become raw List  → same Class, no generic overload
  instanceof List<String>  ──►  illegal ; only instanceof List<?>
```

```
  ┌──────────────┐  List<? extends Account>  ┌──────────────────┐

  │ Service      │  (read-only sum)           │ totalBalance()   │

  └──────────────┘  newEntity() reflectively  └──────────────────┘      └────────────┘

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Erasure Restrictions + PECS ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Type Token (Class<T>): recover erased type for instantiation   │
  │    WHY: new T() is impossible after erasure                    │
  │ Bounded Wildcards (PECS): variance for read vs write safety    │
  │    WHY: accept subtypes to read, supertypes to write           │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ L: SavingsAccount substitutes Account wherever producer reads  │
  │ O: new entity type = new Class token, no code change           │
  │ D: utility depends on Account/wildcards, not concrete subtypes │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Erasure Makes Impossible (as prose) ───────────────────────
  new T()                 : T erased → no constructor known (use Class token)
  instanceof List<String> : element type gone → only List<?>
  new T[n]                : arrays reified vs generics erased → conflict
  overload by generic     : both erase to raw List → signature clash

  ── PECS (as prose) ───────────────────────────────────────────
  ? extends T : PRODUCER — read as T, cannot add (unknown exact subtype)
  ? super  T  : CONSUMER — add T, read only as Object (unknown supertype)
  exact   T   : both read and write

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. repo = new GenericRepository<>(Account.class)
  2.   → newEntity() → token.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()
  3. totalBalance(List<? extends Account>) → read sum = 1,250,000
  4. addSavings(List<? super SavingsAccount>) → write SAV9999
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Type erasure is the compiler's process of using generic type information to check my code at compile time and then removing it, replacing each type parameter with its bound, or with Object when it is unbounded, and inserting casts where needed. The practical consequence is the single fact that explains everything else: at runtime a List of String and a List of Integer are the same class, plain List, because the element type is gone. So generics are a compile-time safety feature with zero runtime cost.

That one fact makes several things impossible. I cannot write new T, because at runtime T is erased to its bound and the JVM does not know which constructor to call, so the standard workaround is to pass a Class token and construct reflectively. I cannot write instanceof on a parameterized type like List of String, because the runtime only sees List with no memory of the element type, so I can only test instanceof List of question mark. I cannot create a generic array like new T of some size, because arrays are reified and carry their component type for runtime store checks, which directly conflicts with erased generics. And I cannot overload two methods that differ only by generic type argument, such as one taking a List of String and one a List of Integer, because after erasure both have the same raw signature and clash.

PECS, Producer Extends Consumer Super, is the rule for wildcard bounds and it follows directly from variance. A List of question mark extends T is a producer, so I can safely read every element as a T, but I cannot add anything except null because the exact subtype is unknown. A List of question mark super T is a consumer, so I can safely add T values because they fit any supertype, but when I read I only get Object back. So if a parameter is a source I read from I use extends, if it is a sink I write into I use super, and if I both read and write I use an exact type with no wildcard. The classic example is Collections.copy, which reads from an extends source and writes to a super destination.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this showed up constantly. A generic repository could not use new T, so it took an entity Class token and created instances reflectively. A reporting utility summed balances over a List of question mark extends Account so it could accept a list of SavingsAccount and read every element as an Account, and an onboarding utility wrote new savings records into a List of question mark super SavingsAccount so it could add into a list typed to Account or any supertype. The senior point I always make is that erasure is exactly why I sometimes carry a Class token or a type reference to recover type information at runtime, and why I occasionally see unchecked-cast warnings, and that getting the PECS wildcard wrong is one of the most common sources of confusing cannot-be-applied compile errors in real generic APIs.
